0001 [# ] Möbius : A Unified Motion-Language Model Bridging Understanding and Generation
0002 [# ] Abstract
0003 [TEXT abstract1.1] We aim to build a truly unified motion model that can understand, generate, and edit human motion within a single framework. Existing motion UMMs remain only partially unified: motion understanding is handled by a language model, while generation is often delegated to a separate diffusion module operating over learned motion latents. We introduce Möbius , which brings the entire diffusion process into the same multimodal representation space used for motion understanding. Clean motion, noisy motion, and text jointly participate in shared attention, while role-specific parameters process understanding and generation streams. Importantly, Möbius operates directly on continuous frame-level raw motion, requiring neither discrete tokenization nor a pretrained motion VAE. This simple formulation naturally supports motion captioning, text-to-motion generation, temporal completion, and instruction-guided editing within a single model. On HumanML3D, Möbius achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified motion models. Scaling to 1.7B parameters and 1,700 hours of motion data further demonstrates that our framework is both effective and scalable.
0004 [TEXT ] Figure 1: Multi-turn motion creation with Möbius . A motion sequence is progressively generated, completed, edited, and understood through natural language in multiple turns.
0005 [# ] 1 Introduction
0006 [TEXT S1.p1.1] Unifying understanding and generation within a single model is a central goal of multimodal intelligence, including motion-language modeling. Existing approaches have largely followed two paradigms. Diffusion-based methods ( Tevet et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) excel at high-fidelity motion generation but typically lack native motion understanding capabilities. In contrast, language-model-based approaches ( Guo et al., 2022b ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) unify multiple motion–language tasks autoregressively, but struggle in generation quality. This gap motivates a unified model that excels at both understanding observed motion and generating high-fidelity motion from natural-language instructions.
0007 [TEXT S1.p2.1] Recent unified motion–language models have attempted to unify motion understanding and generation ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) (see Fig. 2 for an architectural comparison). In these approaches, the language model first produces a shared multimodal representation, which is then passed as conditioning to an external diffusion model for motion generation. While this design allows understanding and generation to interact through a common feature space, the actual denoising process remains largely separated from the language model. The unified representation specifies what motion to generate, but does not directly participate in how the motion is progressively constructed. Consequently, motion understanding and motion generation are only partially unified. This motivates a more tightly integrated formulation in which not only the conditioning representation, but also the diffusion process itself operates within the unified multimodal feature space. We therefore ask: Can motion understanding and the entire motion generation process be unified within a single representation space?
0008 [TEXT S1.p3.1] To address this question, we introduce Möbius , which brings the entire motion diffusion process into the same unified representation space as motion understanding. Both clean motion for understanding and noisy motion under generation are represented as motion tokens and jointly participate in the same attention with language tokens. Inspired by the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) ( Liang et al., 2024 ) design, we use dedicated parameters to process clean and noisy motion streams while allowing them to communicate through shared attention. As a result, motion generation is no longer performed by an external diffusion module conditioned on features produced by the language model. Instead, noisy motion is progressively denoised directly within the unified multimodal space, where it can continuously interact with clean motion and language semantics. The generated motion can in turn be fed back as clean motion tokens for subsequent understanding and reasoning, forming a fully unified loop between motion generation and understanding. This tighter integration leads to stronger motion generation, understanding, and cross-modal interaction within a unified model.
0009 [TEXT S1.p4.1] A key advantage of this formulation is that it removes the need to learn an intermediate motion latent space. Rather than relying on a pretrained motion VAE, tokenizer, or task-specific encoder ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , Möbius operates directly on raw motion representations. Clean motion used for understanding and noisy motion used for generation share the same representation interface: both are projected into the unified multimodal space, with their roles distinguished only by whether they represent clean observations or noisy states undergoing denoising. This makes motion understanding and generation two modes of computation over the same underlying motion representation, rather than two tasks connected through separately learned latent spaces. The resulting framework is considerably simpler, requiring no additional representation learning stage or pretrained motion encoder, while our experiments show that directly modeling raw motion is sufficient to achieve strong performance for both understanding and generation.
0010 [TEXT S1.p5.1] To preserve the generalization ability of the pretrained LLM used in Möbius , we adopt a curriculum training strategy. Joint training can introduce interference between understanding and generation, as gradients from the generation objective can propagate into the understanding parameters through shared attention. We therefore first train on motion understanding tasks, allowing the LLM to acquire meaningful motion semantics, and then introduce the generation objective on top of this learned representation. This curriculum training strategy provides a stable foundation for generation while better preserving the model’s original generalization ability.
0011 [TEXT S1.p6.1] We evaluate two model variants to assess benchmark performance and the benefits of scaling model capacity and training data. Under the HumanML3D evaluation protocol ( Guo et al., 2022a ) , Möbius -0.6B achieves state-of-the-art results in both text-to-motion generation and motion captioning, outperforming relevant diffusion-based, language-model-based, and motion–language baselines. Möbius -0.6B also demonstrates strong capabilities in motion completion, motion in-betweening, and instruction-guided editing. Controlled ablations substantiate the effectiveness of our reasoner–generator architecture, showing that coupling motion understanding and generation yields improvements over commonly used architectural alternatives. We further present Möbius -1.7B, a larger variant trained on 1,700 hours of high-quality motion data, which delivers additional improvements across all motion-language tasks on both controlled and uncontrolled user inputs.
0012 [# ] 2 Related Work
0013 [TEXT ] Figure 2: Architectural comparison of unified motion–language modeling paradigms. (a) Language-based motion models discretize motion into tokens and model motion and text within a shared LLM. (b) Continuous motion–language models use the LLM to produce conditioning representations, while motion is generated by an external diffusion module. (c) Möbius brings the denoising process into the unified multimodal backbone, allowing noisy motion and language to interact throughout generation.
0014 [# ] Unified Multimodal Models.
0015 [TEXT S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Unified multimodal models bring understanding and generation into a shared framework, as exemplified by recent systems such as BAGEL ( Deng et al., 2025 ) and Cosmos3 ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . Existing approaches adopt unified sequence modeling ( Chameleon Team, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) or hybrid objectives combining text autoregression with visual denoising ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . Mixture-of-Transformers introduces modality-specific computation with shared attention ( Liang et al., 2024 ) , while task-decoupled architectures further address interference between understanding and generation ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . These developments motivate our investigation of specialized computation within a unified motion–language model.
0016 [# ] Human Motion Modeling.
0017 [TEXT S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Human motion research spans diffusion-based generation ( Tevet et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024a ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , discrete-token generation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2025 ) , retrieval and understanding ( Petrovich et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , editing and completion ( Athanasiou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025d ; Cohan et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , and spatial control ( Wan et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . These methods are typically developed for particular tasks, with objectives and conditioning mechanisms tailored to their settings. Generalist frameworks consolidate multiple motion synthesis tasks ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Cong et al., 2026 ) , motivating broader unification that also incorporates language-based motion understanding.
0018 [# ] Unified Motion Understanding and Generation.
0019 [TEXT S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Motion–language models support understanding and generation through discrete motion vocabularies ( Guo et al., 2022b ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025c ; Zhou et al., 2024b ) , with extensions to conversational and multimodal interaction ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Ling et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . Continuous alternatives avoid discrete quantization: MoTe ( Wu et al., 2024 ) and UniMotion ( Li et al., 2025a ) jointly model motion and text through latent diffusion, while MotionGPT3 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , LLaMo ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and UniMotion ( Wang et al., 2026 ) integrate continuous motion representations with language-model backbones for unified understanding and generation. These approaches avoid discrete motion tokens but still rely on learned motion latent spaces or encoder–decoder interfaces. Möbius instead operates directly on framewise motion features and brings denoising into the unified multimodal backbone. Clean motion, noisy motion, and text share attention, while role-specific projectors and Transformer parameters specialize their processing. This allows noisy motion to continuously interact with motion and language context throughout denoising.
0020 [# ] 3 Method
0021 [TEXT S3.p1.1] Möbius unifies motion understanding and generation within a shared representation space (see Figure 3 ). Starting from frame-level raw motion (Section 3.1 ), Möbius routes clean and noisy motion tokens to role-specific parameters while allowing them to interact through shared attention (Section 3.2 ). It further adopts a curriculum training strategy to establish a stable foundation for generation while preserving the model’s original generalization ability (Section 3.3 ).
0022 [TEXT ] Figure 3: Overview of Möbius . Motion understanding and generation share a unified multimodal backbone. Text tokens, clean motion frames, and noisy target frames with flow time $t$ participate in shared attention at every layer, while role-specific parameters handle normalization, projections, and feed-forward transformations. The text head autoregressively predicts captions, and the motion head recovers target frames in parallel for generation, temporal completion, and editing. The central matrices illustrate attention visibility for motion understanding and generation.
0023 [# ] 3.1 Frame-level raw motion representation
0024 [TEXT S3.SS1.p1.1] In our framework, we choose frame-level raw motion as the motion representation instead of learning any additional motion encoder. In previous methods, discrete motion tokenizers introduce quantization error ( Guo et al., 2022b ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) , while VAE-based approaches compress motion to temporally downsampled latents ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , losing frame-level information. Instead, we follow HY-Motion ( Wen et al., 2025 ) to represent a motion clip as $X=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}$ with motion token dimension $D{=}201$ comprising joint positions and rotations. Special tokens $\langle\mathrm{BOM}\rangle$ and $\langle\mathrm{EOM}\rangle$ are used to delimit the motion token sequence from text. Two dedicated projectors map clean motion tokens and noisy motion tokens to the shared representation space for understanding and generation, and corresponding motion heads decode it back to the raw motion space. In comparison with existing methods ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) that learn different encoders for understanding and generation, we show that the raw motion representation can achieve strong performance in a unified representation space.
0025 [# ] 3.2 Unified feature space attention with MoT
0026 [TEXT S3.SS2.p1.1] To process all the clean or noisy raw motion and text prompts, we adopt a Mixture-of-Transformers ( Liang et al., 2024 ) structure. In MoT, tokens are routed to different parameters for normalization and linear projection but are then processed by a unified attention operation. We introduce how we route different tokens, and then we discuss how to conduct generative denoising.
0027 [# ] Routing scheme.
0028 [TEXT S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We route tokens based on their roles. Text tokens, boundary tokens, and clean motions are intended for understanding and are processed by the understanding parameters. Noisy target motions are used for generation and thus processed by the generation parameters
0029 [TABLE_ROW ] | $r_{i}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{gen},&i\text{-th token is a noisy motion token},\\ \mathrm{und},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$ | | (1)
0030 [TEXT S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] where $r_{i}$ determines the set of parameters used in normalization and linear projection (“to QKV" in standard attention layers). After that, all projected tokens are processed by a shared attention operation to exchange information in the same feature space.
0031 [# ] Bidirectional attention for motion.
0032 [TEXT S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] In our design, motion token attention follows a different bidirectional visibility pattern from the causal attention of autoregressive text tokens. Specifically, we allow all motion tokens within the same motion sequence to attend bidirectionally to one another, regardless of whether they represent clean motion for understanding or noisy motion for generation. For understanding, the entire observed motion is already available as input, so bidirectional attention enables each frame to capture context from the complete motion sequence. For generation, all noisy target frames are instantiated jointly at each denoising step, and bidirectional attention allows each frame to exploit both past and future temporal context during refinement. Text tokens, in contrast, retain the causal attention pattern of the pretrained language model. In implementation, the target generated motion sequence is always put at the end of the whole sequence with its generation sequence length specified before denoising, allowing the full noisy sequence to be progressively refined as a whole.
0033 [# ] 3.3 Curriculum training strategy
0034 [TEXT S3.SS3.p1.1] We train Möbius in two stages. Directly optimizing motion understanding and generation together is unstable, as the randomly initialized generation pathway can disrupt the pretrained language representations and degrade the model’s understanding ability. We therefore adopt an understanding-first training strategy: the model first learns to interpret motion in the language space, and generation is introduced only after this representation has been established.
0035 [# ] Phase I: motion understanding.
0036 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We initialize our model from Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and train it together with the motion projector on motion captioning. Given a clean motion sequence $X$ , an instruction $C$ , and a target response $Y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L})$ , we use the standard autoregressive language modeling objective:
0037 [TABLE_ROW ] | $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{und}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(X,C,Y)}\left[\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\log p_{\theta_{\mathrm{und}}}(y_{j}\mid y_{<j},C,X)\right].$ | | (2)
0038 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] This stage allows the pretrained LLM to acquire motion semantics while preserving its original language reasoning capability.
0039 [# ] Phase II: motion generation.
0040 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We then initialize the generation parameters from the trained understanding parameters and freeze the understanding parameters. For a target motion $X_{\mathrm{gt}}$ , we sample $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and $t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]$ , and construct a noisy motion
0041 [TABLE_ROW ] | $X_{t}=(1-t)\epsilon+tX_{\mathrm{gt}}.$ | | (3)
0042 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2] The model is trained to iteratively denoise $X_{t}$ to recover the clean motion while attending to the frozen text and motion representations produced by the understanding part:
0043 [TABLE_ROW ] | $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{\theta_{\mathrm{gen}}}(X_{t},t;H_{\theta_{\mathrm{und}}}(C))-X_{\mathrm{gt}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right].$ | | (4)
0044 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.3] This staged training lets generation build on an already learned motion–language representation, avoiding interference with the pretrained understanding capability.
0045 [# ] Unified motion editing and completion.
0046 [TEXT S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] The same framework naturally extends to a broad range of motion editing and completion tasks by treating the source motion as part of the conditioning context and generating the desired target motion. We also train our model on these tasks. Depending on which parts of the source are observed, the model supports temporal completion, including prediction, backcasting, in-betweening and keyframe infilling. It also supports semantic editing, where a source motion is modified according to a natural-language instruction. In all cases, the observed source motion is encoded as clean context, while the generation process predicts the missing or edited target motion. We construct diverse training pairs covering these settings and jointly train a unified editing model without introducing task-specific architectures.
0047 [# ] 4 Experiments
0048 [# ] 4.1 Experimental Setup
0049 [TEXT S4.SS1.p1.1] We evaluate Möbius on text-to-motion generation, motion captioning, instruction-guided editing, and temporal completion tasks, and conduct controlled ablations to examine its key design choices. Bold and underlined metric numbers indicate the best and second-best performance respectively.
0050 [# ] Text-to-motion generation and motion captioning.
0051 [TEXT S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We consider two model scales: Möbius -0.6B and Möbius -1.7B. The standard 0.6B variant is trained exclusively on HumanML3D ( Guo et al., 2022a ) , while the 1.7B variant additionally uses an internal training corpus containing 1,700 hours of annotated motion. For the generation task, we use the MS-272 evaluator introduced by MotionStreamer ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) to compare against representative baselines from diffusion-based models ( Tevet et al., 2022 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) , autoregressive models ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) , and unified motion-language models ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . For motion captioning, we follow the TM2T protocol ( Guo et al., 2022b ) to compare with those methods that natively support understanding ( Guo et al., 2022b ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) .
0052 [# ] Motion editing and completion.
0053 [TEXT S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] For editing and completion tasks, we report the performance on MotionLab ( Guo et al., 2025 ) benchmark of both Möbius -0.6B trained on HumanML3D ( Guo et al., 2022a ) and an additional variant that incorporates MotionFix ( Athanasiou et al., 2024 ) data in training. The compared baselines include the task-specific baseline MotionFix ( Athanasiou et al., 2024 ) , the generalist model MotionLab ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , and also the unedited source motion.
0054 [TEXT ] Figure 4: Qualitative results on motion understanding and generation. (a) Text-to-motion generation results of HY-Motion ( Wen et al., 2025 ) (yellow), Möbius (blue), and MotionMillion ( Fan et al., 2025 ) (purple). (b) Motion-to-text understanding compared with MotionGPT3 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . (c) Instruction-based editing: source (gray), Möbius (blue), and MotionLab ( Guo et al., 2025 ) (green). (d) Temporal completion: prediction, backcasting, in-betweening, and keyframe infilling; known and generated frames are orange and blue, respectively.

0087 [# ] Results.
0088 [TEXT S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] As shown in Table 1 , Möbius -0.6B outperforms both generation-specialized and unified baselines trained on HumanML3D. The scaled Möbius -1.7B also achieves strong performance against large-scale motion models, attaining the best R-Precision, FID, and MMDist among the compared methods. For motion understanding, Möbius consistently outperforms existing unified motion-language models across all reported metrics (Table 2 ). Furthermore, Möbius surpasses editing-specialized baselines and even the unedited source motion (Table 3 ), demonstrating strong instruction-following capabilities.
0089 [# ] Analysis.
0090 [TEXT S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We attribute our advantages in motion generation to the unified architecture. The routing scheme brings the entire motion diffusion process into the shared representation space, allowing the semantics of clean motion and language to continuously guide generation. Meanwhile, the curriculum training strategy helps preserve the reasoning ability inherited from the pretrained LLM, resulting in strong motion-understanding performance. Together with the frame-level raw motion representation, these designs also enable framewise control and editing that follow language instructions well, improving performance across motion–language tasks without sacrificing one capability for another.
0091 [# ] 4.3 Qualitative Evaluation
0092 [TEXT S4.SS3.p1.1] Figure 4 illustrates the versatility of Möbius across both motion understanding and generation tasks. For text-to-motion generation, Möbius follows challenging multi-part prompts while preserving their temporal ordering. For motion-to-text captioning, it captures the key actions and their temporal progression more accurately. For instruction-guided editing, it modifies the target motion while preserving the surrounding source content. Temporal completion requires no task-specific architecture: changing which frames are treated as observed is sufficient to support motion prediction, backcasting, in-betweening, and keyframe infilling. Across these settings, the same frame-level representation supports both motion understanding and flexible conditional generation.
0093 [TEXT ] Table 4: Ablation study. We study motion encoding, routing, and understanding–generation training. † allows denoising to access only the final-layer context representations; ‡ randomly initializes the denoising parameters instead of transferring those learned during understanding. Their M2T scores equal those of the full model and are not ranked. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best variants, excluding GT.

0102 [TABLE_ROW S4.T4.8.9] 6 | Role | Frame | Gen. only | – | – | – | – | 0.7877 | 0.9486 | 6.0073 | 14.2763
0103 [TABLE_ROW S4.T4.8.10] 7 | Role | Frame | Und. $+$ Gen. | 0.5291 | 0.4941 | 0.3929 | 0.3801 | 0.8125 | 0.9506 | 8.0030 | 14.1169
0104 [TABLE_ROW S4.T4.8.11] 8 | Role | Frame | Und. $\to$ Gen. † | 0.6001 | 0.5670 | 0.5629 | 0.4507 | 0.7621 | 0.9387 | 5.7644 | 14.5591
0105 [TABLE_ROW S4.T4.8.12] 9 | Role | Frame | Und. $\to$ Gen. ‡ | 0.6001 | 0.5670 | 0.5629 | 0.4507 | 0.7721 | 0.9422 | 5.8772 | 14.5665
0106 [TABLE_ROW S4.T4.8.13] 10 | Role | Frame | Und. $\to$ Gen. | 0.6001 | 0.5670 | 0.5629 | 0.4507 | 0.8207 | 0.9571 | 4.8772 | 14.0269
0107 [# ] 4.4 Ablation Studies
0108 [TEXT S4.SS4.p1.1] We ablate the motion encoding, routing strategy, and understanding–generation training in Table 4 . All variants use Qwen3-0.6B, are trained on HumanML3D using only the T2M and M2T objectives, and use MS-272 from MotionStreamer ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) as the underlying motion feature format. For motion encoding, VQ discretizes motion using a tokenizer trained following MotionGPT ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , VAE maps motion into the pretrained latent space of MotionStreamer, and Frame directly models framewise MS-272 features without an intermediate motion codec. For routing, Dense uses a single parameter set for all tokens, Modality separates text and motion computation but uses the same motion parameters for both clean observations and noisy denoising states, while Role (ours) assigns role-specific parameters to text/clean motion and noisy motion while retaining shared attention. For training, Gen. only trains generation without understanding pretraining, Und. $\to$ Gen. first establishes motion–language understanding and then transfers it to generation, Gen. $\to$ Align $\to$ Joint follows the MotionGPT3 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) schedule, and Und. $+$ Gen. jointly optimizes both objectives.
0109 [TEXT S4.SS4.p2.1] Which motion encoding best supports unified modeling? We compare three representative motion interfaces in IDs 1, 2, and 10. Since discrete VQ tokens do not naturally represent intermediate continuous denoising states, the VQ variant uses dense computation, whereas the VAE and frame-level variants support role-specific processing of clean and noisy motion. VQ substantially weakens generation, while VAE remains competitive but yields weaker motion understanding than direct frame-level encoding. Overall, frame-level modeling provides the strongest balance between the two capabilities. Moreover, its one-to-one correspondence between motion frames and model positions naturally supports temporal completion and frame-conditioned manipulation.
0110 [TEXT S4.SS4.p3.1] Should computation be separated by modality or by role? With modality routing, the understanding-only model (ID 3) performs normally, but using the same motion parameters for both clean observations and noisy denoising states (ID 4) causes understanding to collapse. The generate–align–joint schedule (ID 5) largely recovers understanding, but at a substantial cost to generation quality. In contrast, separating clean and noisy motion by computational role (ID 10) maintains strong performance in both directions, indicating that the two roles benefit from specialized parameters while still interacting through shared attention.
0111 [TEXT S4.SS4.p4.1] How should understanding be transferred to generation? IDs 6–10 further isolate how learned motion–language understanding benefits generation. Compared with generation-only training (ID 6), the full model (ID 10) shows that establishing motion–language understanding first provides a stronger foundation for synthesis. Joint optimization (ID 7) notably degrades understanding, revealing interference between the two objectives when optimized together. Restricting denoising to only the final-layer context representations (ID 8) also weakens generation, demonstrating the benefit of layer-wise interaction throughout the denoising process. Randomly initializing the denoising parameters (ID 9) further degrades performance relative to initialization from the parameters learned during understanding. Together, these results support our understanding-first strategy: first establish motion–language alignment, then transfer it to generation through parameter initialization and layer-wise interaction while keeping the learned understanding parameters fixed.
0112 [# ] 5 Discussion and Conclusion
0113 [TEXT S5.p1.1] We presented Möbius , a unified motion–language model that organizes computation by role rather than modality. Its role-routed architecture and continuous frame-level motion interface support motion understanding, generation, editing, and temporal completion within a single unified framework. The results also highlight the benefit of transferring learned motion understanding to generation. Experiments on HumanML3D show strong T2M and M2T performance, while scaling to 1.7B parameters and 1,700 hours of motion data further demonstrates the effectiveness of the design at larger scale.
0114 [TEXT S5.p2.1] More broadly, Möbius demonstrates that understanding and continuous motion generation need not be connected through a separate latent generator, but can instead operate together within a shared multimodal representation space. Our current experiments focus on controlled single-person motion settings. Future work will extend Möbius toward multi-person interaction, more detailed hand and finger motion, retargeting across heterogeneous body structures, and deployment in embodied systems such as real-world robots.
0115 [# ] AI use statement
0116 [TEXT S5.SSx1.p1.1] Generative AI tools were used only to improve the readability and language of the manuscript, including grammar, phrasing, and stylistic editing. They were not used to develop the research methodology, design experiments, implement methods, generate or modify data, formulate mathematical claims, or interpret experimental results. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted edits and take responsibility for the final content of the paper.

0118 [# ] Appendix A Experimental Details and Inference
0119 [TEXT A1.p1.1] This supplement provides experimental and inference details, evaluation protocols, and additional results.
0120 [# ] A.1 Datasets
0121 [TEXT A1.SS1.p1.1] Möbius -0.6B uses HumanML3D motion–text data, while the 1.7B model additionally uses an internal corpus of approximately 1,700 hours. The editing variant adds MotionFix pairs during Phase II. Pure-text examples are interleaved during Phase I; “HumanML3D-only” refers to the source of motion–text supervision, not the absence of language pretraining or replay.
0122 [# ] A.2 Continuous Motion Interface
0123 [TEXT A1.SS2.p1.1] We use 201-dimensional HY-Motion features at 30 FPS: pelvis translation (3), root orientation in a continuous 6D representation (6), local body rotations (126), and root-relative joint positions (66). Each frame occupies one Transformer position. Let $\mu,\sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{201}$ denote the training-set feature statistics, and define the elementwise scale $\tilde{\sigma}=\max(\sigma,\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon>0$ . Normalization and its inverse are
0124 [TABLE_ROW ] | $\bar{x}_{i}=(x_{i}-\mu)\oslash\tilde{\sigma},\qquad x_{i}=\bar{x}_{i}\odot\tilde{\sigma}+\mu,$ | | (5)
0125 [TEXT A1.SS2.p1.2] where operations are elementwise. All flow equations in the paper operate in this normalized space.
0126 [TEXT A1.SS2.p2.1] For observed motion, $P_{\mathrm{und}}$ denotes the framewise mapping before output normalization and learned scaling:
0127 [TABLE_ROW ] | $z_{i}=P_{\mathrm{und}}(\bar{x}_{i}),\qquad h_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=m_{i}\,s\frac{z_{i}}{\max(\|z_{i}\|_{2},\varepsilon)}+(1-m_{i})e_{[\mathrm{M}]},\qquad s=\min(\exp(b),s_{\max}).$ | | (6)
0128 [TEXT A1.SS2.p2.2] Here $m_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ indicates whether a source frame is visible, $b$ is learned, and $e_{[\mathrm{M}]}$ represents an unrevealed frame. Noisy targets use $h_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{\mathrm{gen}}(X_{t,i})+e(t)$ and are decoded by $\widehat{X}_{i}=P_{\mathrm{out}}(g_{i})$ , where $g_{i}$ is the final-layer hidden state at target position $i$ , computed using the generation parameters. The projector architectures, scale cap, and numerical constants are recorded in Table S1 .
0129 [TEXT ] Table S1: Architecture specification of Möbius .

0132 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.3] Vocabulary size | 151,673 | 151,673
0133 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.4] Total parameters | 1.047B | 3.148B
0134 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.5] Motion representation | HY201, 30 FPS | HY201, 30 FPS
0135 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.6] Transformer layers | 28 | 28
0136 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.7] Hidden dimension | 1,024 | 2,048
0137 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.8] Query heads | 16 | 16
0138 [TABLE_ROW A1.T1.4.9] KV heads | 8 | 8

0161 [# ] A.3 Task Construction
0162 [TEXT A1.SS3.p1.1] Let $C$ be the text instruction, $B_{S}$ an observed-motion span, $B_{t}$ the noisy target span, and $Y$ a text response. The mask $m$ controls which source frames are provided as clean context to the understanding parameters. Task-specific context is summarized in Table S3 .
0163 [TEXT ] Table S3: Unified task construction. $\Omega$ denotes observed temporal indices. For temporal tasks, observations use the target timeline.
0164 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.1] Task | Context / output | Observed motion
0165 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.2] T2M | $C\rightarrow B_{t}$ | None
0166 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.3] M2T | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow Y$ | Full source
0167 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.4] Editing | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow B_{t}$ | Full source
0168 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.5] Prediction | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow B_{t}$ | Prefix $\Omega$
0169 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.6] Backcasting | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow B_{t}$ | Suffix $\Omega$
0170 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.7] In-betweening | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow B_{t}$ | Prefix and suffix
0171 [TABLE_ROW A1.T3.4.8] Keyframe infilling | $[C,B_{S}]\rightarrow B_{t}$ | Sparse frames
0172 [TEXT A1.SS3.p2.1] For editing, the source is supplied only as understanding context; the target starts from Gaussian noise, as in T2M. Temporal tasks also provide observed frames through the understanding context, without pinning generated frames after sampling updates. Their observation masks and initialization settings are specified with the evaluation protocol below.
0173 [# ] A.4 Inference
0174 [TEXT A1.SS4.p1.1] The model predicts a clean endpoint using the generation parameters. Text-only classifier-free guidance retains the same motion context in both passes. Here $f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;C,S,m)$ abbreviates the endpoint predictor with context encoded using the understanding parameters, and $\theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{und}},\theta_{\mathrm{gen}})$ :
0175 [TABLE_ROW ] | $\widehat{X}_{g}(X_{t},t)=f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\varnothing,S,m)+w\bigl[f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;C,S,m)-f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\varnothing,S,m)\bigr].$ | | (7)
0176 [TEXT A1.SS4.p1.2] The source is absent for T2M. For a grid $0=t_{0}<\cdots<t_{N}=1$ , Euler sampling converts the predicted endpoint to a velocity:
0177 [TABLE_ROW ] | $X_{t_{n+1}}=X_{t_{n}}+(t_{n+1}-t_{n})\frac{\widehat{X}_{g}(X_{t_{n}},t_{n})-X_{t_{n}}}{\max(1-t_{n},\varepsilon)}.$ | | (8)
0178 [TEXT A1.SS4.p1.3] The network is evaluated at $t_{n}<1$ , and the final motion is denormalized. Because context cannot attend to noisy targets, its layer-wise keys and values can be reused across sampling steps; conditional and null-text passes use separate caches.
0179 [TEXT A1.SS4.p2.1] For M2T, the model uses the understanding parameters to generate $p(Y\mid C,S)=\prod_{j}p(y_{j}\mid y_{<j},C,S)$ autoregressively. Pure-text inference uses the same parameters without a motion span. Sampler and text-decoding settings are listed in Table S4 .
0180 [TEXT ] Table S4: T2M and M2T inference-pipeline settings. The response-token limit is the M2T script default. Editing and temporal-inpainting conditions are specified separately in their task protocols.
0181 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.1] Setting | Text-to-motion | Motion-to-text
0182 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.2] Sampler / decoder | Euler with clean-endpoint-to-velocity conversion | Autoregressive greedy decoding
0183 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.3] Steps / time grid | 50; uniform on $[0,1]$ ; timestep shift $1.0$ | Not applicable
0184 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.4] CFG scale | $3.0$ | Not applicable
0185 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.5] Initialization / input | Standard Gaussian noise | Observed clean motion
0186 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.6] Motion length | Reference length, clipped to $[2,300]$ frames at 30 FPS | Input motion length
0187 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.7] Response limit / stopping | Not applicable | 128 new tokens; stop at the configured EOS token
0188 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.8] Text sampling | Not applicable | Disabled; temperature $0$
0189 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.9] Prompt | “Generate a complete motion from the following description:” followed by the caption | “Describe this motion:” with the motion input
0190 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.10] Random seed | $42+i$ , with $i$ the original protocol index | Deterministic decoding
0191 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.11] Weights | EMA | EMA
0192 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.12] Evaluation passes | One in the inspected evaluation records | One in the inspected evaluation records
0193 [TABLE_ROW A1.T4.4.13] Output handling | Denormalize HY201 and convert to the evaluator representation | Decode up to <|im_end|> ; strip surrounding whitespace
0194 [# ] A.5 Inference Efficiency
0195 [TEXT A1.SS5.p1.1] Table S5 reports single-GPU measurements for both model sizes with EMA weights and BF16 autocast. T2M uses 50 Euler steps, CFG 3.0, and separate conditional/unconditional passes. M2T uses greedy decoding with EOS stopping and a limit of 128 new tokens; actual output lengths are reported because they affect decoding latency. The fixed inputs are the first eight captions in the T2M evaluation protocol and the first eight eligible M2T motions in sorted ID order, cropped to 150 frames. Batch-one measurements use the first input in each set. Timing includes context encoding and generation, with CUDA synchronization around each call. Model loading, dataset I/O, motion conversion, smoothing, and rendering are excluded. These repeated-input measurements characterize inference cost rather than average latency over the full test set.

0206 [# ] Appendix B Metrics and Evaluation Protocols
0207 [# ] B.1 Evaluation Protocols
0208 [# ] Text-to-motion.
0209 [TEXT A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We evaluate on 4,042 selected-caption HumanML3D test cases using the MotionStreamer MS-272 evaluator ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) . Generated motions are converted to the evaluator representation, and text–motion retrieval uses candidate batches of 32.
0210 [# ] Motion-to-text.
0211 [TEXT A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We follow the TM2T protocol ( Guo et al., 2022b ) , comprising 4,400 cases: 3,969 full motions and 431 temporal subclips. Each case has three reference captions. Linguistic metrics use the raw reference captions; semantic retrieval uses the HumanML3D matching network with candidate batches of 32.
0212 [# ] Editing and temporal completion.
0213 [TEXT A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Editing follows the MotionLab protocol ( Guo et al., 2025 ) on MotionFix, with the unchanged source included as a no-edit baseline. Temporal completion covers prediction, backcasting, in-betweening, and keyframe infilling, corresponding to the observation patterns in Table S3 . Comparisons use matched sample IDs, observations, target lengths, and text conditions. Motions are converted to HumanML3D-263 where required by the evaluator.
0214 [# ] B.2 Evaluation Metrics
0215 [TEXT A2.SS2.p1.1] Table S6 summarizes the metrics and their preferred directions. Embedding-based scores depend on the task-specific evaluator and should not be compared across different embedding spaces. For temporal completion, MPJPE and [P]-MPJPE distinguish motion reconstruction from preservation of observed frames; [P] does not denote Procrustes alignment.
0216 [TEXT ] Table S6: Meaning of the evaluation metrics. $\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$ indicate preferred directions; $\rightarrow$ indicates closeness to the real-data value.
0217 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.1] Metric | Definition and interpretation
0218 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.2] R@ $k$ $\uparrow$ | Fraction of queries whose paired target ranks among the top $k$ candidates in the task-specific embedding space. Ranks are computed within the candidate set of the corresponding protocol.
0219 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.3] FID $\downarrow$ | Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits to generated and real motion embeddings; measures distributional agreement.
0220 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.4] MMDist / MM-D $\downarrow$ | Mean paired text–motion embedding distance for T2M/M2T; the editing table uses motion–motion distance. This is not maximum mean discrepancy.
0221 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.5] M2M-Dist $\downarrow$ | Mean distance between generated and target motion embeddings for editing.
0222 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.6] AvgR $\downarrow$ | Mean rank of the paired target in editing retrieval; depends on candidate-set size.
0223 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.7] Diversity $\rightarrow$ | Mean embedding distance between sampled motion pairs; compare with the real-data reference.
0224 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.8] BLEU-1 / BLEU-4 $\uparrow$ | Reference-based n-gram precision with brevity penalty.
0225 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.9] ROUGE-L $\uparrow$ | Reference-based longest-common-subsequence overlap.
0226 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.10] CIDEr $\uparrow$ | Consensus-weighted n-gram agreement with reference captions.
0227 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.11] BERT $\uparrow$ | Contextual-token semantic agreement, reported as rescaled BERTScore F1.
0228 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.12] MPJPE $\downarrow$ | Mean Euclidean distance between predicted and reference joint positions over the evaluated frames.
0229 [TABLE_ROW A2.T6.4.13] [P]-MPJPE $\downarrow$ | Joint-position error on observed/preserved frames; here [P] means preservation, not Procrustes alignment.

0237 [# ] C.3 Motion Knowledge Question Answering
0238 [TEXT A3.SS3.p1.1] Table S7 presents text-only probes of motion knowledge and motion-language instruction generation. Base and ours receive the same English questions without any motion input. These examples probe motion-related knowledge and instruction generation without motion input, complementing the motion-conditioned captioning evaluation.
0239 [TEXT ] Table S7: Qualitative comparison on motion-knowledge QA and motion-language instruction generation. All questions are text-only and require no motion input.
0240 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.1] | Base | Ours
0241 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.2] Q1. How does the body’s height change when stepping up versus stepping down?
0242 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.3] Answer | When stepping up, the body moves upward as the person lifts the leg and pushes onto the higher surface. When stepping down, the body moves downward as the person lowers the foot to the lower surface and transfers their weight onto it. | The body’s center of mass rises when stepping up and lowers when stepping down, following the change in support height.
0243 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.4] Q2. What happens to the knee and hip joints when a person squats down?
0244 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.5] Answer | As a person squats down, both the knees and hips bend to lower the body. The knees move forward while the hips move backward, allowing the person to descend while maintaining balance. | Both the knees and hips flex as the body lowers, with increasing joint flexion toward the bottom of the squat.
0245 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.6] Q3. Why is it harder to maintain balance when hopping on one foot than when jumping on both feet?
0246 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.7] Answer | Hopping on one foot is more difficult because the body has only one foot supporting its weight. This provides less stability and requires more coordination to keep the body upright, whereas using both feet gives a more stable base of support. | One-foot hopping has a smaller support area, requiring tighter control of the center of mass to remain balanced over the supporting foot.
0247 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.8] Q4. Generate three random text instructions that could be used for text-to-motion generation.
0248 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.9] Answer | 1. Walk forward naturally for a few steps, as if approaching something in front of you. 2. Try a simple jumping movement where you bend your legs, push yourself off the ground, and then land again. 3. Slowly turn your body toward the left while moving your arms naturally with the motion. | 1. A person walks forward three steps and turns to the left. 2. A person crouches down, touches the ground, and stands back up. 3. A person jumps forward and lands with both knees bent.
0249 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.10] Q5. What kind of movement is Tai Chi, and how is it typically performed?
0250 [TABLE_ROW A3.T7.4.11] Answer | Tai Chi is a traditional Chinese martial art known for its slow, gentle, and controlled movements. It is typically performed as a sequence of flowing postures, with an emphasis on relaxation, balance, breathing, and coordination. Practitioners move continuously from one posture to another in a calm and deliberate manner. | Tai Chi uses slow, continuous movements with smooth weight shifts, gradual torso rotations, and coordinated curved motions of the arms.
0251 [# ] C.4 Temporal Completion
0252 [TEXT A3.SS4.p1.1] Table S9 reports results under four observation patterns. The 0.6B model achieves the lowest MPJPE in all four tasks, while the 1.7B model achieves the lowest FID throughout. For example, in prediction, our MPJPE reaches 7.177 compared with the best baseline’s 8.781; in keyframe infilling, our best FID is 0.286 compared with 0.358. Observed-frame preservation remains task-dependent: HY-Motion has the lowest [P]-MPJPE for prediction and Kimodo for in-betweening, whereas our models lead for backcasting and keyframe infilling. These results show complementary strengths in reconstruction and distributional quality, rather than a uniform advantage on every metric. The two model sizes also use different training data, so their comparison does not isolate model scale.
0253 [# ] Effect of multi-task training on T2M and M2T.
0254 [TEXT A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Table S8 compares the main-table 0.6B model with the multi-task variant after 20k continuation steps. Adding conditional generation tasks yields a modest T2M trade-off: R@1 decreases by 1.53 percentage points, FID increases from 6.1291 to 6.6746, and MMDist increases from 13.9973 to 14.0824. Nevertheless, the multi-task model still outperforms all other HumanML3D-trained methods in Table 1 on R@1–3, FID, and MMDist, including generation-specialized models. Its M2T scores remain identical to the main-table results, consistent with keeping the understanding parameters frozen during the additional generation training.
0255 [# ] Why report two training variants?
0256 [TEXT A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] The main-table comparison focuses on the bidirectional T2M/M2T setting shared with unified motion–language baselines, reducing the influence of additional task-specific supervision on that comparison. The multi-task evaluation asks a complementary question: can the same architecture accommodate additional observation patterns and conditional generation objectives while retaining its core capabilities? The temporal-completion results, together with the strong T2M scores and unchanged M2T performance, support this broader task coverage without introducing task-specific generation modules. We therefore report the variants separately to make the trade-off between task breadth and T2M specialization explicit. This demonstrates extensibility across trained tasks, rather than establishing zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or distributions.
